newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil reform drive seen facing formidable hurdles.
newsitem.headline: Brazil reform drive seen facing formidable hurdles.

text.p: Brazil watchers were skeptical Wednesday about whether President Fernando Henrique Cardoso could use his new political clout to speed passage of economic reforms that were shelved months ago.
"Cardoso will definitely have some momentum now, but how much? This is not going to solve all the reform problems," said Gene Frieda, an analyst at I.D.E.A. consulting firm in New York.
Cardoso, confident after a key congressional victory late Tuesday in his bid for re-election, told lawmakers on Wednesday that he wanted them to take up the reforms as early as next week.

Still, even Cardoso supporters admitted reforms were unlikely to be discussed before mid-February. Economists said the reform agenda looked no less ambitious on Wednesday than it did before the re-election debate knocked it off the political map last October.

"Losing would have been disastrous," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Barings in Brazil, referring to the re-election vote. "But I am not so euphoric because it doesn't really improve chances" for accelerating economic reforms.
"It maintains the status quo so you essentially have the same chances of getting reforms passed as you did before the re-election discussion arose," Schneider added.

Economists say the reforms, aimed at revamping civil service and pension law, are needed to keep Brazil securely on its path toward economic stability. They warn that gains in slowing inflation during the past three years could be jeoparidized by out-of-control federal spending, which can only be tamed by constitutional reforms.

Political commentators argue that the eventual passage of a re-election amendment, seen likely after the vote Tuesday in the lower house of Congress, should give Cardoso the political strength to accelerate his reform program.
Economists were much more skeptical, noting that the reforms would hit the pocketbooks of average Brazilians, making the proposals politcally unpopular in Congress.

"By the time they get re-election approved there will be only a few months before the government has to start slowing down the economy to deal with the (trade deficit)," I.D.E.A.'s Frieda said. "So are they going to be able to get congressmen to vote for benefit cuts as the economy slows and 1998 elections loom?"

Pension reform, which would affect all Brazilians, is a much more prickly issue. The government's original bill was watered down last year, and economists said Cardoso, with or without a re-election amendment under his belt, would not be able to push through a stronger version.
"We might see pension reform getting passed by the end of the year, but it will be nothing close to the real deep reform the government originally wanted," Schneider said.
